title: LESKO: Feasibility and Preliminary Effectiveness of Dog-Assisted Psychotherapy in a Group Therapy Setting. Dog-Assisted Group Psychotherapy for Children with Expansive Behavior Disorders: Luna’s Trail – Enhancing Emotional and Social Competencies
summary:
Disruptive behavior problems are among the most common disorders in childhood and adolescence. Affected children and adolescents often show deficits in empathy, impulse control, and emotion regulation. They frequently struggle to maintain attention, self-regulation, and motivation to participate in therapeutic interventions such as social skills training. The targeted use of certified therapy dogs can help to motivate children and adolescents to engage in the therapeutic process, interact productively with their therapists, and maintain motivation throughout the course of therapy.
Animal-assisted interventions have furthermore demonstrated positive effects on socio-emotional and cognitive development, self-esteem, empathy, and the assumption of responsibility. One underlying mechanism is that interactions with therapy dogs elicit emotional responses and activate attentional networks, thereby enhancing learning processes during therapy. Based on this assumption, the inclusion of a therapy dog could serve as a catalyst for social learning.
Studies from English-speaking countries have shown a reduction in disruptive symptoms in children who participated in dog-assisted group psychotherapy programs. To date, there is no standardized manual for conducting dog-assisted group psychotherapy for children with disruptive behavior disorders in German-speaking countries. Within the present study, a manualized dog-assisted group psychotherapy program was developed to promote social and emotional competencies in children with disruptive behavior problems.
The study aims to examine the feasibility and acceptance, as well as the preliminary effects, of a dog-assisted group therapy program in (partial) inpatient child and adolescent psychiatric treatment. The research questions will be investigated within the framework of a feasibility study.
A total of N = 24 children aged 9 to 13 years with disruptive behavior disorders will be included. Feasibility will be assessed through dropout rates, adherence, and response rates, while acceptance will be evaluated using satisfaction ratings on Likert scales. Preliminary effectiveness will be measured through pre- and post-assessments of disruptive behavior, empathy, and prosocial behavior based on standardized parent- and child-report questionnaires. The resulting findings may contribute to tailoring treatment approaches more specifically for children with disruptive behavior problems.
conditions: Mixed disorders of conduct and emotions

interventions.name: A total sample of 24 children is planned in the clinical cohort. Participants will take part in a weekly training program based on a standardized and manualized dog-assisted group therapy intervention involving a certified therapy dog. The patients are in partial or inpatient psychiatric treatment a

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Clinical diagnosis of a disruptive behavior disorder (ICD-10: F90.0, F90.1, F91, F92).
Exclusion criteria:
Exceeding or falling below the specified age range, as well as refusal to participate by either the parents or the child.
Further exclusion criteria include insufficient ability to speak and read German fluently, intellectual disability (IQ ≤ 70), allergy to dog hair, or fear of dogs.
